topics.title: MVC, Folder Structure, Config and Environments
topics.summary: Organise code into routes, controllers, services and models, centralise config, and keep one codebase for dev, test and production.
topics.description:
A single `index.js` works for demos; real APIs need structure so teams can find and change code safely.

### Layers (separation of concerns)
| Layer | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| **Routes** | map URL + method to a controller; attach middleware (auth, validation) |
| **Controllers** | read `req`, call a service, shape the `res` - no business rules |
| **Services** | business logic, orchestration, transactions - no `req`/`res` |
| **Models / repositories** | database access and schemas |
| **Middleware** | cross-cutting concerns (auth, errors, logging) |
| **Utils / config** | helpers, env loading, constants |

This is **MVC** adapted for APIs: the "view" is simply the JSON response.

### Recommended folder layout
Two common styles: **by type** (`controllers/`, `models/`, `routes/`) for small apps, and **by feature** (`modules/users/{user.routes.js, user.controller.js, user.service.js, user.model.js}`) for larger ones - everything about a feature lives together.

### Config module
Read `process.env` in **one** file, validate it, export a frozen object, and import `config` everywhere else. Do not scatter `process.env.X` through the code.

### Environments
Use `NODE_ENV` (`development`, `test`, `production`) and separate env files or platform variables per stage: different database URIs, secrets, log levels and CORS origins. Always set `NODE_ENV=production` in production: Express then caches views and error handling is leaner.

### Dependency direction
Routes -> controllers -> services -> models. Lower layers never import upper layers.
keyPoints: Routes -> controllers -> services -> models; no skipping or reverse imports
Controllers handle HTTP only; services hold business rules
Organise by feature as the app grows
One validated config module; no scattered `process.env`
`NODE_ENV` + per-stage variables for dev/test/prod
pitfalls: Fat controllers with database queries and business logic
Services that depend on `req`/`res` (cannot be reused or tested)
Same `.env` used for every stage or secrets committed per stage

interview.a: Controllers translate HTTP; services hold reusable business logic without req/res, which makes it easy to test and reuse from jobs, scripts or other transports.

interview.q: Why centralise process.env access in a config module?
interview.a: It validates required variables once at startup, gives typed defaults, and avoids hidden dependencies on environment variables across the code base.

topics.title: Logging with morgan and pino, Health and Monitoring
topics.summary: Log HTTP requests and application events as structured JSON, correlate them with request ids and expose health checks.
topics.description:
You cannot fix what you cannot see. Production needs useful, safe logs and basic monitoring.

### HTTP request logs: morgan
`morgan('dev')` prints a coloured line per request in development; `morgan('combined')` writes Apache-style access logs. It is a middleware that logs method, URL, status and response time.

### Structured application logs: pino
`console.log` is unstructured and slow. **pino** is a very fast JSON logger with levels (`trace`, `debug`, `info`, `warn`, `error`, `fatal`). JSON lines can be searched and aggregated by Datadog, Loki, CloudWatch or ELK. **pino-http** logs every request as JSON and attaches `req.log`, a child logger that includes the request id. In development use `pino-pretty` for readable output.

### What to log
- Requests (method, path, status, duration), errors with stack traces, auth events (login failures), slow queries, job runs.
- **Never log**: passwords, tokens, full card data, whole request bodies. Use pino's `redact` option for paths such as `req.headers.authorization`.

### Request id
Generate or accept `X-Request-Id`, attach it to every log line and return it in the response, so a user report can be traced across services.

### Health checks
`GET /health` (liveness: process is up) and `GET /ready` (readiness: DB reachable). Load balancers and Kubernetes use them to route traffic and restart pods.

### Monitoring
Track error rate, latency percentiles, memory and CPU. Tools: Sentry (exceptions), Prometheus + Grafana (`prom-client` metrics), Datadog/New Relic (APM), uptime monitors (UptimeRobot, Better Stack).
keyPoints: morgan = HTTP access log; pino = fast structured JSON app logger
Redact secrets; never log passwords or tokens
Request ids tie together all log lines of one request
Provide `/health` (liveness) and `/ready` (readiness) endpoints
Use Sentry or APM for errors and performance
pitfalls: `console.log` everywhere in production (no levels, no structure)
Logging request bodies with credentials
Health check that always returns OK even if the database is down

examples.title: pino-http, request id and health checks
morgan for development

interview.a: JSON logs are machine-searchable and aggregatable (by level, request id, user), unlike free-text console output.
Liveness tells the orchestrator the process is alive (restart if not); readiness says it can serve traffic (dependencies like the DB are reachable), so load balancers route only to ready instances.

topics.title: API Docs with Swagger / OpenAPI
topics.summary: Describe endpoints with OpenAPI and serve an interactive Swagger UI so frontend developers can explore and test the API.
topics.description:
**OpenAPI** (formerly Swagger) is a standard, language-neutral format (YAML/JSON) describing an API: paths, parameters, request/response schemas, auth. **Swagger UI** renders it as an interactive page where you can click "Try it out".

### Why
- Frontend and mobile developers get an always-current contract.
- Clients and tests can be generated from the spec.
- It doubles as living documentation and design review material.

### Two ways to produce the spec
1. **Code-first**: write JSDoc comments (`@openapi` blocks) above routes and let **swagger-jsdoc** collect them.
2. **Spec-first**: maintain `openapi.yaml` manually (or generate from Zod schemas with libraries such as `zod-to-openapi`) and load it.

### Serving it
`swagger-ui-express` mounts the UI: `app.use('/api-docs', swaggerUi.serve, swaggerUi.setup(spec))`. Often exposed only in development/staging, or behind authentication in production.

### Describe
- `servers` (base URL), `components.securitySchemes` (Bearer JWT), `components.schemas` (reusable models like `User`, `Error`), each operation's `summary`, `tags`, `parameters`, `requestBody`, `responses` (200, 400, 401, 404).
- Add `security: [{ bearerAuth: [] }]` to protected routes so the "Authorize" button works.

### Tip
Keep docs close to the route code (or generated from the same schemas) so they do not drift.
keyPoints: OpenAPI = standard contract; Swagger UI = interactive docs
swagger-jsdoc (code-first) or a hand-written spec (spec-first)
Mount UI with `swagger-ui-express` on `/api-docs`
Define reusable `components.schemas` and `securitySchemes`
Protect or disable docs in production if the API is private
pitfalls: Docs drifting from the code because they are written by hand and forgotten
Exposing internal-only endpoints in public docs
Missing `security` on protected operations, so "Try it out" always gets 401

examples.title: swagger-jsdoc + swagger-ui-express

interview.q: What is the difference between Swagger and OpenAPI?
interview.a: OpenAPI is the specification for describing REST APIs; Swagger is the tool family (Swagger UI, Editor, Codegen) that originally defined and now implements it.
Code-first generates the spec from annotations or schemas in code (less drift); spec-first designs the OpenAPI document before coding and treats it as the contract.

topics.title: Response Envelope, Pagination and Versioning Standards
topics.summary: Agree on one JSON shape for success and errors, one pagination format and a versioning policy so clients stay simple.
topics.description:
Consistency is what makes an API pleasant. Decide the rules once and apply them everywhere.

### Response envelope
Wrap responses in a predictable shape:
```json
{ "status": "success", "data": { ... }, "meta": { "page": 1 } }
{ "status": "error",   "message": "Validation failed", "errors": [ ... ] }
```
Pros: clients can add metadata (pagination, request id) without breaking changes, and handle errors uniformly. Some teams prefer returning the bare resource and using HTTP status codes plus a standard error body (RFC 9457 `application/problem+json`). Pick one and be consistent.

### Helpers
Small functions `ok(res, data, meta)`, `created(res, data)` and the central error handler keep controllers tidy and the shape identical.

### Pagination standard
- Request: `?page=2&limit=20` (offset) or `?cursor=abc&limit=20` (cursor).
- Response `meta`: `page`, `limit`, `total`, `totalPages`, plus `hasNext`. Or `Link` headers (`rel="next"`) and `X-Total-Count`.
- Enforce a **maximum limit** and a sensible default.

### Naming and formats
Plural nouns, `camelCase` JSON keys, ISO-8601 dates in UTC, ids as strings, money in the smallest unit (cents/paise), `null` for missing values.

### Versioning policy
Prefix with `/api/v1`. Additive changes (new fields, new endpoints) are non-breaking; removing or renaming fields, or changing semantics, requires `/api/v2`. Announce deprecations with a `Deprecation`/`Sunset` header and keep the old version running for a defined period.
keyPoints: One success shape and one error shape across the API
Pagination metadata in `meta` (page, limit, total, totalPages)
Cap `limit`; support cursor pagination for large feeds
camelCase keys, ISO dates (UTC), money in smallest unit
Breaking change -> new version (`/api/v2`), deprecate with notice
pitfalls: Different shapes per endpoint (arrays here, wrapped objects there)
Returning HTTP 200 with `status: "error"` in the body
Changing field meaning in-place without a version bump

examples.title: Response helpers

interview.q: What is a response envelope and why use it?
interview.a: A fixed wrapper (status, data, meta) around every response; it lets you add metadata like pagination without breaking clients and keeps error handling uniform.

interview.q: When should an API get a new version?
interview.a: When a change would break existing clients, such as removing or renaming fields or altering behaviour; additive changes can ship in the same version.

topics.title: Testing with Vitest/Jest and supertest
topics.summary: Test routes without opening a port using supertest, cover happy and error paths, and isolate the database.
topics.description:
Automated tests protect an API from regressions. For Express the usual stack is a test runner (**Vitest** or **Jest**) plus **supertest**, which sends HTTP requests directly to your `app` object - no `listen()` needed. This is why you export `app` separately from `server.js`.

### Kinds of tests
| Level | What | Tools |
|---|---|---|
| Unit | one function (service, util) with mocks | Vitest/Jest |
| Integration | route + middleware + DB together | supertest + test DB |
| End-to-end | deployed app, real client | Playwright/Cypress/Postman |

### Writing an integration test
1. Import `app`.
2. `await request(app).post('/api/tasks').send({...})`.
3. Assert on status, headers and body.

Test the unhappy paths as much as the happy ones: validation errors (400), missing auth (401), forbidden (403), not found (404), duplicates (409).

### Database in tests
Never touch the development database. Options: **mongodb-memory-server** (in-memory MongoDB), a dedicated test database that is cleaned before each test, or Testcontainers/Docker. Use `NODE_ENV=test` to load test configuration, and reset data in `beforeEach`.

### Mocking
Mock external services (email, Stripe, S3) with `vi.mock` / `jest.mock` so tests are fast and deterministic.

### Auth in tests
Create a user and sign a token in a helper, then call `.set('Authorization', 'Bearer ' + token)`.

### CI
Run `npm test` on every pull request; track coverage but do not chase 100 percent.
keyPoints: supertest sends requests to `app` without a port
Export `app` separately from `listen`
Test error paths (400/401/403/404/409), not only success
Use an isolated test DB (memory server) and reset between tests
Mock external services; run tests in CI on every PR
pitfalls: Tests that depend on each other or on leftover data
Hitting the real development/production database
Leaving the server listening and hanging the test process

examples.title: Vitest + supertest
Setup and run
examples.code:
npm i -D vitest supertest
# package.json -> "scripts": { "test": "vitest run" }
npm test

#  ✓ tests/tasks.test.js (4 tests)
#  Test Files  1 passed (1)
#       Tests  4 passed (4)

interview.q: Why does supertest not need the server to listen on a port?
interview.a: It binds your app to an ephemeral port internally for each request, so you only need to export the Express app, not start a server.

interview.q: How do you keep tests from affecting each other?
interview.a: Use a separate test database, clean or reset data in beforeEach, and avoid shared mutable state between tests.

topics.title: Dockerizing an Express App
topics.summary: Package the API into a small, secure image and run it with MongoDB using docker compose.
topics.description:
**Docker** packages your app with its exact Node version and dependencies into an **image** that runs the same on your laptop, CI and the cloud.

### A good Dockerfile
1. Start from a slim base: `node:24-alpine` (or `-slim`).
2. Copy `package*.json` first and run `npm ci --omit=dev` - Docker caches this layer, so rebuilds are fast unless dependencies change.
3. Copy the source after installing.
4. Set `NODE_ENV=production`, `EXPOSE` the port, and run as the non-root `node` user.
5. Start with `CMD ["node", "src/server.js"]` (exec form) so signals like SIGTERM reach Node and graceful shutdown works. Avoid `npm start` as PID 1.

### `.dockerignore`
Exclude `node_modules`, `.git`, `.env`, logs and tests so the build context is small and secrets are never copied into the image.

### Multi-stage builds
Use one stage to build (TypeScript, dev dependencies) and a final lean stage that copies only the output and production dependencies.

### docker compose
Define the API and its dependencies (MongoDB, Redis) in `compose.yaml`. Services reach each other by service name (`mongodb://mongo:27017/app`). Use a named volume so database data survives container recreation. Pass configuration via `environment:` or `env_file`, never bake secrets into the image.

### Health check
Add a `HEALTHCHECK` (or compose `healthcheck`) hitting `/health`.

### Bind to all interfaces
Inside a container, listen on `0.0.0.0` (the default for `app.listen(port)`), and map the port with `-p 3000:3000`.
keyPoints: Slim base image, `npm ci --omit=dev`, copy `package.json` before source
Run as non-root `node` user with `CMD ["node", ...]`
`.dockerignore` keeps secrets and junk out of the image
Compose wires API + Mongo/Redis; use named volumes for data
Pass secrets at runtime, not at build time
pitfalls: Copying `.env` or `node_modules` into the image
Using `localhost` for the database inside a container (use the service name)
`npm start` as PID 1 swallowing SIGTERM, causing slow or forced shutdowns

examples.title: Dockerfile and compose.yaml
examples.code:
# ---- Dockerfile ----
FROM node:24-alpine
WORKDIR /app
ENV NODE_ENV=production

COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev

COPY src ./src

USER node
EXPOSE 3000
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s CMD wget -qO- http://localhost:3000/health || exit 1
CMD ["node", "src/server.js"]

examples.title: compose.yaml
examples.code:
services:
  api:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
    environment:
      NODE_ENV: production
      PORT: 3000
      MONGO_URI: mongodb://mongo:27017/app
      JWT_ACCESS_SECRET: ${JWT_ACCESS_SECRET}
    depends_on:
      mongo:
        condition: service_healthy
    restart: unless-stopped

  mongo:
    image: mongo:7
    volumes:
      - mongo-data:/data/db
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "mongosh", "--quiet", "--eval", "db.adminCommand('ping')"]
      interval: 10s
      retries: 5

volumes:
  mongo-data:

examples.title: .dockerignore and commands
examples.code:
# .dockerignore
node_modules
.git
.env
npm-debug.log
tests

# build and run
docker compose up --build -d
docker compose logs -f api
docker compose down          # add -v to also delete the database volume

interview.q: Why copy package.json before the source code in a Dockerfile?
interview.a: Docker caches layers; installing dependencies in an earlier layer means they are only reinstalled when package files change, making rebuilds much faster.

interview.q: Why use CMD ["node", ...] instead of npm start?
interview.a: The exec form runs Node as PID 1 so SIGTERM reaches your app for graceful shutdown; npm start adds a wrapper process that may not forward signals.

topics.title: PM2, nginx Reverse Proxy and CI/CD
topics.summary: Run Node under PM2 (cluster mode), put nginx in front for HTTPS and static files, and automate deploys with GitHub Actions.
topics.description:
### PM2: process manager
Node runs on one CPU core and dies on crashes. **PM2** keeps it alive and uses all cores:
- `pm2 start src/server.js -i max` starts one worker per core (cluster mode) sharing the same port.
- Auto-restart on crash, restart on memory limit (`--max-memory-restart 300M`), log management, `pm2 reload` for zero-downtime restarts, `pm2 startup` + `pm2 save` to survive reboots.
- Configure via `ecosystem.config.cjs`.

Cluster mode means in-memory state (sessions, rate-limit counters, caches) is **per worker**, so use Redis or the database for shared state. Containers/Kubernetes often replace PM2: run one process per container and scale containers.

### nginx: reverse proxy
Public traffic hits **nginx** on ports 80/443, which forwards to Node on `localhost:3000`:
- **TLS termination** with Let's Encrypt certificates (certbot).
- Serves the React build and static assets quickly, with gzip/brotli and caching.
- Passes `X-Forwarded-For` / `X-Forwarded-Proto` headers: set `app.set('trust proxy', 1)` in Express.
- Request size limits, rate limiting, WebSocket upgrade headers for Socket.IO.

### CI/CD
**CI** (continuous integration) runs lint and tests on each push; **CD** (continuous delivery) deploys when `main` passes. A GitHub Actions workflow typically: checkout, set up Node with cache, `npm ci`, `npm test`, build/push a Docker image, then SSH to the server (or call the platform's deploy hook) and `pm2 reload`.

Store credentials in GitHub **Secrets**, never in the repository.
keyPoints: PM2 `-i max` = cluster mode across CPU cores, auto-restart, zero-downtime reload
Cluster/multi-instance means shared state must live in Redis/DB
nginx terminates TLS, serves static files and proxies to Node
Set `trust proxy` behind nginx for correct IP and protocol
CI runs tests on every push; CD deploys from main using secrets
pitfalls: Forgetting WebSocket upgrade headers in nginx (Socket.IO falls back or fails)
Running in cluster mode with in-memory sessions
Deploying without running tests, or storing server keys in the repo

examples.title: ecosystem.config.cjs and nginx
nginx site config
GitHub Actions workflow
examples.code:
name: CI-CD
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 24
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test

  deploy:
    needs: test
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Deploy over SSH
        uses: appleboy/ssh-action@v1.0.3
        with:
          host: ${{ secrets.SERVER_HOST }}
          username: ${{ secrets.SERVER_USER }}
          key: ${{ secrets.SERVER_SSH_KEY }}
          script: |
            cd /var/www/my-api
            git pull origin main
            npm ci --omit=dev
            pm2 reload ecosystem.config.cjs --env production

interview.a: Node is single-threaded; cluster mode starts one worker per CPU core to use all cores, restarts crashed workers and allows zero-downtime reloads.

interview.q: What does nginx do in front of Express?
interview.a: It terminates HTTPS, serves static content efficiently, compresses and buffers traffic, applies limits and forwards requests to the Node process.

topics.title: Redis Caching and Performance Tuning
topics.summary: Cache expensive reads in Redis (cache-aside), and apply the main Express performance rules.
topics.description:
### Redis cache-aside
**Redis** is an in-memory key-value store. The most common pattern is **cache-aside**:
1. Build a key (`products:list:page=1`).
2. Try `redis.get(key)`. On a hit, return it immediately.
3. On a miss, query the database, `redis.set(key, JSON.stringify(data), 'EX', 60)`, return.
4. When data changes, **invalidate** (`del`) the affected keys.

Always set a TTL, so stale data eventually disappears. Cache what is read often and changes rarely (product lists, config, expensive aggregations). Do not cache per-user private data under shared keys. Redis is also used for sessions, rate limiting, queues (BullMQ), pub/sub and distributed locks. If Redis is down, the app should fall back to the database, not crash.

### Express performance checklist
- `NODE_ENV=production`.
- Use `compression` (or let nginx do it).
- Never block the event loop: avoid sync functions (`fs.readFileSync`, `bcrypt.hashSync`, big JSON loops) on request paths; move CPU work to worker threads or queues.
- Index database fields used in filters/sorts; paginate; use `.lean()` and field selection; avoid N+1 queries (use `populate`/`$lookup`/`include`).
- Reuse connections (one pool/client).
- HTTP caching: ETag, `Cache-Control`, CDN for static files and public GETs.
- Run multiple processes (PM2 cluster / containers) and scale horizontally.
- Keep payloads small; stream large responses.
- Measure first: `clinic.js`, `autocannon`, APM traces and slow-query logs.
keyPoints: Cache-aside: get -> miss -> DB -> set with TTL -> invalidate on writes
Always use TTLs; handle Redis failures gracefully
Never block the event loop with sync or CPU-heavy code
Index, paginate and avoid N+1 queries
Measure with autocannon/clinic before optimising
pitfalls: Caching without invalidation (users see stale data forever)
Shared cache keys for user-specific responses
Premature optimisation without profiling

examples.title: Cache middleware with ioredis
Load testing
examples.code:
npx autocannon -c 50 -d 10 http://localhost:3000/api/products
# compare "Req/Sec" with and without the cache middleware

interview.a: The application checks the cache first; on a miss it loads from the database, stores the result in the cache with a TTL, and returns it; writes invalidate or update the cached entries.

interview.q: Name common causes of slow Express APIs.
interview.a: Blocking the event loop with sync/CPU work, missing database indexes, N+1 queries, large uncompressed payloads, and creating connections per request.
